subsections.heading: ### Study Design and Data Sources
subsections.replacement:
This retrospective secondary-data study developed a clinical prediction model in one national survey and validated it, without refitting, in another. Reporting follows Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis extended to artificial intelligence (TRIPOD+AI, 2024) [15]. Self-assessed risk of bias (Prediction model Risk Of Bias Assessment Tool, PROBAST) [16] was low-to-unclear overall, driven by complete-case handling of substantial and differential depression-module non-response in the external cohorts (Multimedia Appendix 1, Part D). The protocol and statistical analysis plan, including the four hypotheses, were dated before any analysis; the study was not registered.

Development used the Korea Community Health Survey, a nationwide Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency (KDCA) household survey [17] of community-dwelling adults (~230,000/year) under a stratified, clustered, weighted complex-sample design. The development sample pooled KCHS 2017-2025 records with the PHQ-9 administered (n=2,048,510), split at cluster level (survey year crossed with design stratum crossed with primary sampling unit): the 100,001-record hold-out and the 500,000-record training set share 0 clusters. Training-set size was fixed for tractability before any external evaluation.

External validation used NHANES, an NCHS survey combining household interview and mobile examination center assessment, with depression measured by the Depression Screener (DPQ; PHQ-9) module under the 2015-2018 sample design and estimation procedures [18]. Two periods served as separate validation sets: pre-pandemic (2017-March 2020, "P_" files; n=7,888) and post-pandemic (August 2021-August 2023, "_L" files; n=5,210); documentation and weight variables are named in Multimedia Appendix 1, Part A.

subsections.heading: ### Participants and Outcome
subsections.replacement:
Eligible respondents in both surveys were adults aged 20 years or older with all nine PHQ-9 items answered; pregnant respondents were retained. Pooling KCHS 2017-2025 gave 2,048,510 eligible records, and among examined NHANES adults 7,888 pre-pandemic and 5,210 post-pandemic answered all nine items. Frame counts and item-level non-response are tabulated in Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S8. Predictors and outcome were recorded in the same survey contact, and blinding does not apply to already-collected responses.

The outcome is current depression, a PHQ-9 total of at least 10, computed identically in both surveys (nine items scored 0 to 3, KCHS items recoded 1-4→0-3 to match NHANES). The ≥10 cut-off is the conventional screening threshold, evaluated against semi-structured diagnostic interviews in individual-participant-data meta-analyses [3,19] and validated in a Korean population [20].

subsections.heading: ### Predictors and Harmonization
subsections.replacement:
Only variables reducible to a common definition in both surveys entered the harmonized model of 17 predictors (Table 1). All 616 KCHS concepts were crosswalked against the NHANES codebook for both cycles; a concept was retained if available in NHANES, collected in more than one KCHS survey year, and not circular with the PHQ-9 outcome. Those criteria rest on documentation and availability alone, no NHANES outcome association having been estimated before the amendment below was locked. Retained domains carry established associations with depression: socioeconomic position [21], sleep duration [22], physical activity [23], body mass index (BMI) [24], smoking [25], living alone [26] and partnership status [27].

**Table 1.** Harmonized 17-predictor set shared by the Korea Community Health Survey (KCHS) and the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES).

One representative variable name is shown per concept; several concepts, physical activity in particular, derive from more codes than are shown, and the full year- and cycle-specific crosswalk is in Multimedia Appendix 1. Predictors 15 to 17 entered the set through the documented protocol amendment, and race and ethnicity is not a predictor.
BMI: body mass index.
PHQ-9: 9-item Patient Health Questionnaire.

The 17-predictor set was not pre-specified: the protocol specified 14, and employment, self-rated oral health and household food insecurity were added by an amendment written and dated before any model using those items was fitted, though after the external result for the 14-predictor set was known. Each has an established depression association: food insecurity (pooled odds ratio ≈1.4) [28], unemployment (≈1.9-2.1) [29] and poor oral health (bidirectional) [30]. The seventeen are every eligible concept in the extract available at that point; five further items from a later exhaustive extraction were screened post hoc, none added (Multimedia Appendix 1, Parts A and D).

Living alone, the one retained item absent from the pre-pandemic NHANES file, has no missing values anywhere in the KCHS training data; the tree learner therefore never learns a missing direction for it, and that cohort is scored as if no respondent lived alone. The pandemic-period contrast is repeated without it.

Three harmonization cautions attach to the set: BMI is self-reported in KCHS and measured in NHANES; alcohol, physical activity and income were reduced to conservatively comparable definitions across different instruments; and food insecurity rests on a single KCHS item against the 10-item NHANES module, the weakest link in the set [31].

The preprocessing pipeline handling missing data was fitted in the development training set and applied unchanged to the internal hold-out and to each external set, with no leakage; the one exception is the income quintile, recomputed as a rank-based score within each dataset and each KCHS survey year (Multimedia Appendix 1, Part D).

subsections.heading: ### Model Development and Evaluation
subsections.replacement:
No a priori sample-size calculation was performed; each external cohort is every eligible respondent in that cycle. Available power is reported instead: approximately 18,000 events in the training set, about 1,000 per candidate predictor, and approximately 3,600 in the hold-out. The external cohorts (728 events pre, 661 post; weighted prevalence 8.4% and 12.2%) are the binding constraint on precision; discrimination therefore carries confidence intervals, and subgroup estimates are read as exploratory.

Three algorithms were considered in two selection steps confined to the KCHS training set: penalized logistic regression (elastic net), random forest and gradient boosting (LightGBM). A randomized search over 24 LightGBM configurations crossed with two feature representations (main effects with and without four candidate interaction terms) fixed the gradient-boosting hyperparameters and selected main effects. All three were then tuned over comparable grids under one cross-validation protocol and compared at best configuration, regression being a fair comparator once validation bias is controlled [32].

The analysis plan fixed the primary-model rule in advance: highest cross-validated AUROC, differences below 0.005 treated as ties and broken by proximity of the calibration slope to 1, then by parsimony. The pipeline as executed omitted the tie band, though the plan's rule checked retrospectively reproduces the selected model. No imbalance correction was applied, the learner being fitted on the natural 3.6% event rate; that departure and single-pass rather than repeated 5-fold cross-validation are recorded in Table S9.

No NHANES data were used in fitting, tuning or selecting the primary model; the predictor set is the one exception (Predictors and Harmonization). The in-domain oracle reported under Testing Whether External Discrimination Can Be Raised Above ~0.77 is fitted on NHANES labels by design, as a diagnostic upper bound rather than a candidate model. Complex-survey weights were handled by unweighted training with weighted evaluation.

Performance was summarized, all complex-survey weighted, by discrimination (AUROC and area under the precision-recall curve [AUPRC]), operating characteristics, and calibration, assessed at the moderate level of the calibration hierarchy [33] through the calibration slope, calibration-in-the-large (CITL), the Brier score and expected calibration error (ECE). Ninety-five percent CIs came from a rescaled stratified cluster bootstrap with 1000 replicates [34]; ECE, operating characteristics and net benefit are point estimates, and two-sided bootstrap P values reach P<.001 at the smallest attainable value (Table S16).

A single operating threshold, the predicted probability giving 85% sensitivity (0.02051), was fixed once in the development data and applied unchanged to the hold-out and both external cohorts, hence the external operating characteristics are transported rather than locally selected. Clinical utility was assessed by weighted decision-curve analysis [35] over threshold probabilities of 0.02 to 0.30 (Table S3).

subsections.heading: ### External Validation and Sensitivity Analyses
subsections.replacement:
Geographic transportability was assessed by applying the KCHS-trained model to NHANES without refitting, and period transportability by evaluating the same transported model separately in the pre- and post-pandemic cycles; since development pools KCHS 2017-2025 across both periods, the second comparison contrasts target periods rather than validating a model frozen before the later cycle. Calibration recovery was quantified by out-of-sample intercept and slope updating, which corrects calibration without re-estimating predictor effects [13,14] and is the conventional first step for a transported model [36]. Three updates, cross-fitted over five folds grouped by primary sampling unit, were applied: intercept only, intercept plus slope (recommended, Table 2), and one-parameter temperature scaling with the intercept fixed at zero; the other two appear in the Results.

Three further analyses were undertaken: interpretability, through global tree-based Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) importance [37] and cross-survey rank concordance; fairness, through weighted subgroup AUROC and calibration slope across sex, age, education and, in NHANES, race and ethnicity [38]; and a parsimonious model for a low-burden self-administered form, with predictor order and item count fixed inside the development training set and evaluation reserved to the hold-out and both NHANES cohorts (Multimedia Appendix 1, Part D).

Sensitivity analyses, pre-specified with further analyses added afterwards, varied the outcome cut-off (≥5 as well as ≥10), the predictor set (→14 without the three added predictors, →16 without food insecurity), weighting, imputation, the alcohol definition and an age lower bound of 30 years applied to training and evaluation, and added a continuous-score analysis of the untransformed PHQ-9 total; weighted AUROC is tabulated in Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S5 apart from the continuous-score and alcohol analyses, reported in the Results text. Analyses used Python 3.14 with package versions in the model card; net benefit is reported without intervals, since inference on a decision-analytic quantity answers a different question from the decision itself [39].

An adversarial data-integrity audit corrected three silent data-processing defects before final analysis: a fabricated living-alone constant in NHANES pre-pandemic, a post-pandemic physical-activity parsing error, and an income refusal code (77777) not treated as missing. Peer review identified four further defects (post-pandemic income quintile, 2017 income refusal codes, post-2020 drinking classification, 2018 physical-activity indicator), all corrected in the primary analysis rather than carried as limitations; defects, remedies and six singly quantified corrections are in Multimedia Appendix 1, Part D and Table S10.

subsections.heading: ### Ethical Considerations
subsections.replacement: NHANES data collection was approved by the NCHS Research Ethics Review Board, and KCHS is conducted under the authority of the KDCA; both sources as analyzed are de-identified secondary survey data (see Data Availability). The Institutional Review Board of Daejeon University granted an exemption from review (approval number [to be inserted]) on the grounds that the study uses publicly available de-identified data, records no personal identifiers, and poses no more than minimal risk (Multimedia Appendix 1, Part D). Written informed consent was obtained from every participant by the data-collecting agencies at the time of the original surveys; the present analysis required no additional consent, and none was sought.

appendix_additions.markdown:
### Detail relocated from the trimmed Methods

Supports the Methods subsections Predictors and Harmonization, Model Development and Evaluation, and External Validation and Sensitivity Analyses, and complements the sections above. Nothing here alters any reported estimate; where a value appears both here and in the manuscript, the manuscript is the reporting site.

Crosswalk extract sizes and the post-hoc screen. The crosswalk available when the protocol amendment was written and locked held a 175-variable extract, of which the seventeen predictors are every eligible concept. A later exhaustive extraction identified 265 variables common to both NHANES cycles, and five further harmonizable items from that extraction were screened post hoc against NHANES outcome associations. None was added, and the predictor set is unchanged (Part A).

Food insecurity across the two countries. A direct Korea-US comparison using the same 18-item household food-security module found food insecurity associated with higher odds of PHQ-9 depression in both countries, with a larger association in Korea [31]. The single-item KCHS measure used here is therefore the weakest link in the harmonized set rather than a difference in the underlying construct. Scale differences between the surveys and questionnaire discontinuities within KCHS were corrected in the analytic data before the primary analysis rather than carried as limitations, as itemized above and quantified singly in Table S10.

Sample size and comparability of the two algorithm searches. The training set supplies about 1,000 events per candidate predictor, far above conventional events-per-predictor requirements. Only gradient boosting received the preceding feature-representation and hyperparameter search, hence the algorithm comparison is like-for-like at each algorithm's tuned best configuration rather than equal in cumulative search effort. The four candidate interaction terms did not improve cross-validated discrimination, and the main-effects representation was selected. Running the searches single-pass rather than as 5-fold cross-validation repeated five times matters here, given that the two leading algorithms differ by less than the tie band of the pre-specified selection rule (Table S9).

Parsimony selection. Predictor order and item count were both fixed inside the development training set, split into a 450,000-record fitting set and a 50,000-record selection set. Predictors were entered in descending order of global SHAP importance, the model was refitted at every item count from 1 to 17, and the count was chosen on selection-set AUROC by the analysis plan's margin, the smallest set within 0.02 AUROC of the full model; the variant using a stricter 0.01 margin is flagged as post hoc. Table S6 gives the full item-count trajectory.

Decision-curve construction and intended use. Each dataset carries its own screen-all and screen-none default strategies in the decision-curve analysis, and the reported net benefit is therefore internal to each cohort (Table S3). The model is intended as a triage aid for population-level screening programs and web or mobile self-assessment services, operated by public-health and primary-care services rather than by individuals acting alone, to prioritize who receives a full PHQ-9 and clinical follow-up; it is not a diagnostic instrument.

sections.verdict: The trim is sound in structure and keeps every item on the DO NOT LOSE list: the 17-versus-14 predictor provenance with the dated locked amendment (strengthened, since the replacement now states in the Methods that the amendment postdates the external result for the 14-predictor set, a fact the current draft buries in Model Development), the living-alone absence and its zero-scoring consequence, the no-NHANES-in-fitting statement with the predictor set flagged as its one exception, the oracle as diagnostic upper bound rather than candidate model, the differential depression-module non-response driving complete-case handling, the four hypotheses, and all ten TRIPOD+AI Methods items. Cross-references are mostly improved rather than degraded: the current draft points PROBAST, the split procedure and the ethics detail at Part B, whereas all three live in Part D (appendix5_methods.md), and the replacement corrects each. Tables S3, S5, S8, S9, S10 and Part A citations all resolve to content that exists. Eight problems remain, one of them a mis-pointed table citation and three of them provenance or evidential claims that shifted: the NHANES sample-design attribution now asserts that the 2017-2023 validation cycles ran under the 2015-2018 design, reference 32 has been repurposed from an empirical finding to a methodological justification, the continuous-score analysis has migrated from protocol-specified to post-hoc in direct conflict with the Results, and the three recalibration updates have lost their pre-specified status. Two facts vanish outright, the count of alternative alcohol definitions and the KCHS interview mode and cadence, and two definitional items are orphaned, the Spearman concordance statistic and the reason ECE carries no interval. All eight are repairable inside the sentences already written, without adding material length.

subsections.heading: ### Participant Characteristics
subsections.replacement:
The pooled KCHS development sample comprised 2,048,510 adults and the external cohorts 7,888 pre-pandemic and 5,210 post-pandemic NHANES adults, similar in mean age (49.4, 48.4 and 48.8 years) and in proportion female (50.5%, 51.5% and 50.8%) but not in outcome frequency. Weighted depression prevalence (PHQ-9 ≥10) was 3.6% in KCHS against 8.4% and 12.2% in the two NHANES cycles (Figure 1). Measured covariates differed as sharply: mean BMI 23.7 against 29.8 and 29.7, and weighted food-insecurity prevalence 3.7% in KCHS vs 16.4% and 17.2% in the NHANES cycles among respondents with the item recorded (missing 22.1%, 6.0% and 6.3%; Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S4 uses available-case denominators throughout).

On the mobile examination center (MEC) frame, which supplies the depression module and the weights used throughout, 7.7% of 8,544 pre-pandemic and 14.1% of 6,064 post-pandemic examined adults aged ≥20 years were lost to PHQ-9 item non-response, yielding the complete-case analytic samples of 7,888 and 5,210. Non-response was differential, higher among respondents with less than high-school education and among Asian and Black respondents; hence the external cohorts, and particularly the post-pandemic fairness estimates, should be read as complete-case results (Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S8).

subsections.heading: ### Model Development and Internal Performance
subsections.replacement: Under the identical tuning protocol, cross-validated AUROC in the training set was 0.840 for LightGBM, 0.835 for random forest and 0.822 for elastic net. The two leading algorithms fell inside the analysis plan's 0.005 tie band, which the calibration-slope tie-break resolves in favor of LightGBM (cross-validated slope 1.00 against 1.20), while elastic net lay outside it (Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S9). Internal hold-out AUROC was 0.836 (95% CI 0.827-0.846), AUPRC 0.246, Brier 0.030, calibration slope 1.03, CITL +0.10; H1 met. The split being at cluster level, this is an estimate for clusters the model never saw.

subsections.heading: ### External Validation Across Country and Pandemic Period
subsections.replacement:
External discrimination fell by about 0.07 AUROC from the internal estimate and differed little between the two cycles: pre 0.765 (95% CI 0.724-0.804), post 0.771 (0.739-0.801) (Table 2; Figures 2 and 3); the difference is +0.006 (95% CI -0.045 to +0.056; bootstrap P=.86), computed after the fact, no between-cycle test having been pre-specified. AUPRC moved in the opposite direction (Table 2), which follows from the higher external event rate: each value should be read against its own no-skill baseline of 3.6%, 8.4% and 12.2%. Calibration degraded in both cycles, the slope falling to 0.65 (pre) and 0.68 (post) and CITL rising to +0.51 and +1.13, indicating that the Korea-trained model systematically *under*-predicted absolute risk in the US (KCHS 3.6% vs 8.4% and 12.2%). Of the three pre-specified recalibration steps applied out-of-sample, intercept-plus-slope updating restored both slope and CITL (Table 2), intercept-only updating removed the mean bias but left the slope unchanged (0.65 pre, 0.68 post), and temperature scaling was intermediate (Multimedia Appendix 1, Part C); intercept-plus-slope is the recommended deployment update; H2 and H3 supported.

AUPRC: area under the precision-recall curve.
ECE: expected calibration error.
CITL: calibration-in-the-large; positive values denote under-prediction of observed risk.

subsections.heading: ### Testing Whether External Discrimination Can Be Raised Above ~0.77
subsections.replacement:
Leakage-controlled optimization (2,199 recorded runs across 117 experiment files spanning feature engineering, hyperparameter search, ensembling, transfer-robust internal selection, domain adaptation, alternative losses and structural variants) did not exceed external AUROC ~0.77 when model selection was restricted to KCHS-internal criteria; apparent gains from externally tuned variants did not survive leakage control (Multimedia Appendix 1, Tables S11 and S12).

The ceiling was localized with an in-domain oracle, a diagnostic upper bound rather than a candidate model: NHANES was fitted on its own labels, cross-validated with folds split by primary sampling unit within each cycle. Across logistic, penalized-logistic, histogram-gradient-boosting and LightGBM learners the oracle reached only 0.764-0.776 (best learner 0.776, 95% CI 0.753-0.799; widening to 0.745-0.794 when the oracle is refitted inside each bootstrap replicate; Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S15). The KCHS-transferred model (pre 0.765, post 0.771) therefore sits inside the confidence interval of the best in-domain performance any of these learners reached on NHANES itself.

Matching sample size did not close the gap: reduced to the NHANES sample size and cross-validated within Korea, the same 17 predictors still yielded 0.823 at n=7,888 and 0.810 at n=13,098 (the pooled oracle size), ie, 0.81-0.82 against an NHANES ceiling of ~0.77, and 0.830 only at n=200,000 (best of three learners, 5-fold weighted AUROC). Three further checks agreed: density-ratio reweighting of the KCHS training sample toward the NHANES covariate distribution (labels unused) *reduced* external AUROC, to 0.766 and 0.758 against the in-run baseline of 0.772 pre and 0.769 post (Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S11); increasing the KCHS training set from 0.5 million to 2 million records did not raise external discrimination; and adding the remaining harmonized-but-unused survey items changed external AUROC by at most 0.003 in either direction. Deep tabular learners (two multilayer perceptrons, TabNet and an FT-Transformer) all fell below gradient boosting internally, and none exceeded it on both external cohorts (Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S13). None of these closed the gap, which recalibration cannot close either, correcting calibration rather than rank ordering.

subsections.heading: ### Parsimonious Deployment Model
subsections.replacement: Predictor order and item count were both fixed inside the training set, and the analysis plan's margin (the smallest set within 0.02 AUROC of the full model) selected six items: self-rated health, age, sex, sleep duration, self-rated oral health, partnership. Evaluated afterwards on data that played no part in selection, this six-item form achieved hold-out AUROC 0.822, NHANES pre 0.748 and NHANES post 0.757, against 0.837/0.766/0.769 for the full 17-predictor model fitted on the same data (a loss of 0.015 internally, 0.018 pre-pandemic and 0.012 post-pandemic, each within the plan's 0.02 tolerance); H4 supported. On the selection set, discrimination rose steeply and then flattened (1 item 0.741; 3 items 0.781; 5 items 0.813; 6 items 0.818; 8 items 0.825; 12 items 0.832; 17 items 0.833), the margin being applied over every count below 17 without imposing the plan's preferred 5-10 item range. The five-item set falls 0.0002 below the threshold and the six-item set clears it by 0.0044; the five-versus-six boundary is therefore decided at the fourth decimal and should not be read as robust, the five-item model reaching 0.737 pre-pandemic and 0.751 post-pandemic externally. The stricter-margin seven-item variant is exploratory only, and no external information entered the item-count decision (Multimedia Appendix 1, Tables S2, S3 and S6).

subsections.heading: ### Sensitivity Analyses
subsections.replacement:
Discrimination was stable across specifications that alter modeling choices rather than the target condition (Figure 4): weighted training (0.836/0.764/0.768 internal/pre/post), missing-indicator imputation (0.837/0.764/0.772) and single chained-equations imputation of the continuous predictors (0.837/0.763/0.770) all lay close to the primary model. Restricting both training and evaluation to respondents aged ≥30 years *improved* discrimination (0.838/0.781/0.787); restricting training alone gave 0.836/0.770/0.769, placing most of that improvement in the evaluation case mix rather than in what the model learned. Changing the outcome definition to PHQ-9 ≥5 lowered discrimination throughout (0.761/0.735/0.740) at a much higher weighted prevalence (15.6%/25.0%/32.1%); notably, the Korea-US gap narrows from about 0.07 AUROC at the ≥10 threshold to about 0.02 at ≥5 (0.761 vs 0.735-0.740). Alternative alcohol definitions, and each harmonization correction applied singly against the uncorrected baseline, changed weighted AUROC by at most 0.003 in any cohort (Multimedia Appendix 1, Tables S5 and S10).

The harmonized set is also robust to its least-established members: refitting without employment, self-rated oral health and food insecurity, each model given its own hyperparameter search, lowers external discrimination to 0.745 (pre) and 0.757 (post), a difference of Δ+0.020, 95% CI +0.010 to +0.030 and Δ+0.014, 95% CI +0.006 to +0.020 (P<.001 for both; paired rescaled cluster bootstrap). In the pre-specified continuous-score analysis a classifier of the deployed specification ranked the untransformed PHQ-9 total with weighted Spearman ρ=0.378 internally, 0.403 pre-pandemic and 0.439 post-pandemic, and a model trained on the continuous score performed similarly (ρ=0.402/0.403/0.424; weighted R² 0.216/0.166/0.102); the pattern is not an artifact of dichotomizing the outcome.

Living alone is absent from the pre-pandemic NHANES file, hence that cohort is scored as if no respondent lived alone, and the pandemic-period contrast mixes a period difference with a predictor-availability difference. Refitting on the 16 predictors observed in both cycles leaves the contrast unchanged: external AUROC 0.765 pre-pandemic and 0.771 post-pandemic, a difference of +0.006 (95% CI -0.044 to +0.056) against +0.006 (-0.045 to +0.056) for the 17-predictor model, with internal discrimination 0.836 against 0.836. Response-propensity weighting by the inverse of each cohort's education-specific module response rate moved external AUROC by at most 0.002 (0.765 vs 0.765 pre-pandemic, 0.769 vs 0.771 post-pandemic).

subsections.heading: ### Interpretability, Fairness, and Clinical Utility
subsections.replacement:
Global SHAP importance ranked self-rated health (0.59) first, followed by age, sex, sleep duration, self-rated oral health, partnership and smoking, with food insecurity modest (0.06, ranked 10th); the items carrying most of the signal are measured identically in both surveys (Figure 5). Rank ordering was highly concordant between KCHS and both NHANES cycles (Spearman ρ=0.97 pre, 0.99 post), an attribution that observes no external outcome. The clearest exception was food insecurity, on which the transported model leaned substantially harder externally (mean absolute SHAP 0.06 in KCHS against 0.18 and 0.15 in the NHANES cycles), consistent with its different measurement and much higher US prevalence.

Subgroup discrimination in KCHS spanned 0.781-0.882 (weighted AUROC): sex (female 0.826, 95% CI 0.814-0.837; male 0.838, 0.822-0.854), education (0.811-0.882), age (20-39 years 0.808, 0.790-0.827 < 40-59 years 0.822, 0.801-0.842 < ≥60 years 0.860, 0.850-0.870), and household income quintile (0.781-0.835, lowest in the highest-income quintile). In NHANES, discrimination was lower and far less precisely estimated. Pre-pandemic: Mexican American 0.693 (0.633-0.763), non-Hispanic Black 0.762 (0.727-0.805), other/multiracial 0.764 (0.665-0.865), non-Hispanic White 0.769 (0.715-0.818), other Hispanic 0.773 (0.725-0.820), non-Hispanic Asian 0.807 (0.716-0.874). Post-pandemic: Mexican American 0.692 (0.533-0.802), non-Hispanic Black 0.726 (0.642-0.791), non-Hispanic White 0.773 (0.726-0.815), other/multiracial 0.782 (0.701-0.853), other Hispanic 0.789 (0.751-0.845), non-Hispanic Asian 0.845 (0.656-0.987). The analysis plan's 0.05 fairness flag was tripped by the highest income quintile in KCHS (-0.056), Mexican American respondents in both cycles (-0.072 pre, -0.078 post) and non-Hispanic Asian respondents post-pandemic (+0.074). Every NHANES interval overlaps the cohort-level interval, hence the race and ethnicity ordering is not established differential performance (Figure 6). Internal subgroup calibration was good, whereas external subgroup slopes were below 1 and subgroup CITL positive in all but one subgroup each, confirming under-prediction of absolute risk rather than only over-extreme ranking (Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S7).

On decision-curve analysis the model gave positive net benefit exceeding both defaults across a clinically relevant threshold-probability range in all three datasets (Figure 7). At a threshold probability of 0.10, net benefit was +0.028 pre-pandemic and +0.058 post-pandemic after intercept/slope updating, against +0.010 internally, in each case above screen-all (-0.017, +0.024 and -0.072). The operating threshold was fixed once in the development data at 85% sensitivity and applied unchanged thereafter, hence the external operating characteristics are transported rather than guaranteed by construction. At that single threshold, sensitivity/specificity were 0.833/0.665 internally, 0.810/0.566 in NHANES pre and 0.791/0.596 in NHANES post, with positive predictive value 0.147 and 0.214 externally (number needed to screen 6.8 and 4.7) and negative predictive value 0.970 and 0.953; the model flagged 47% of the pre-pandemic and 45% of the post-pandemic population. The flagged share follows from where the threshold is set: at 0.10 and 0.15 it falls to 27% and 16% pre-pandemic and to 40% and 26% post-pandemic (Multimedia Appendix 1, Tables S1, S2 and S3). Clinical utility remains provisional pending prospective evaluation.

### Results detail relocated from the manuscript (sample composition, module non-response, predictor attribution, subgroup detail, and the six-item operating point)

Explanatory prose condensed out of the Results is preserved here in full. No new result is introduced.

The contrast between the development and external samples in body-mass index, food insecurity and outcome frequency is consistent with genuinely distinct populations and, for food insecurity, with the single-item-versus-module measurement difference set out in Part A.

Denominator choice governs the apparent size of depression-module non-response. Counted on the mobile examination center frame, which is where the module is administered and on which every weighted estimate in this study is computed, the three-or-more-item non-response rates are 7.4% pre-pandemic and 13.3% post-pandemic. Counted over all interviewed adults the same rates are 14.3% and 32.7%; that second denominator conflates module non-response with never having been examined, which the examination-center weights already account for. Non-response was higher among respondents with less than high-school education, at 12.9% pre-pandemic and 26.6% post-pandemic on the examination-center frame.

Respondents missing only one or two depression items can be recovered by filling the missing items with the person-mean. Doing so changed the observed prevalence by no more than 0.1 percentage points in either cycle (unweighted: 9.23% to 9.27% pre-pandemic, 12.69% to 12.78% post-pandemic), indicating that the complete-case restriction does not itself shift the observed outcome frequency. Item-level counts are in Table S8.

Mean absolute SHAP values for the predictors ranked immediately below self-rated health in the development fitting partition were age 0.37, sex 0.28, sleep duration 0.26, self-rated oral health 0.23, partnership 0.19 and smoking 0.17. Food insecurity ranked 10th in KCHS but 8th in NHANES pre-pandemic; the item is a single question in KCHS against the 10-item module in NHANES.

Analytic subgroup sizes for the external race and ethnicity estimates were, pre-pandemic, Mexican American n=914, non-Hispanic Black n=2,096, other or multiracial n=381, non-Hispanic White n=2,798, other Hispanic n=813 and non-Hispanic Asian n=886; and post-pandemic, Mexican American n=330, non-Hispanic Black n=598, non-Hispanic White n=3,215, other or multiracial n=340, other Hispanic n=499 and non-Hispanic Asian n=228.

Within KCHS a few subgroup intervals sit clear of the cohort interval: higher in adults aged ≥60 years (0.850-0.870) and in middle-school-educated respondents (0.861-0.902); lower in income quintile 4 (0.772-0.822) and in the highest income quintile (0.744-0.818). Subgroup discrimination is therefore not uniform in the development population. That the lowest external point estimate falls in Mexican American respondents in both cycles warrants monitoring as an equity caveat even though the external intervals are mutually overlapping.

Internal subgroup calibration slopes ran 0.96-1.13 across sex, age, education and income strata, with subgroup calibration-in-the-large from -0.03 to +0.20. External subgroup slopes were below 1 in every subgroup except non-Hispanic Asian respondents post-pandemic (0.57-0.79; 1.19 in that subgroup), and external subgroup calibration-in-the-large was positive in every group except Mexican American respondents pre-pandemic, reaching +1.32. Exact values with intervals are in Table S7.

At a within-cohort operating point fixed to 85% sensitivity (apparent values, Table S2), the six-item deployment form required 7.9 pre-pandemic and 5.7 post-pandemic respondents screened per case detected, against 7.7 and 5.3 for the 17-predictor model, and its net benefit exceeded both default strategies in every cohort at threshold probabilities of 0.10 and 0.15 (Table S3).

Replacing current drinking with drinking at least twice weekly, with binge drinking, or with all three indicators together reached 0.769-0.771 pre-pandemic and 0.770 post-pandemic against an in-run baseline of 0.772 and 0.769; that run predates the data-integrity corrections and the cluster-level split, hence its levels are not comparable with the primary estimates or with Table S5. No single tabulated harmonization correction, the age top-code alignment and the rank-based income-quintile rebuild included, changed weighted AUROC by more than 0.003 in any cohort (Table S10).

Under the common configuration of Table S5, in which the 17-, 16- and 14-predictor models share one setting and the 14-predictor value is 0.758 post-pandemic, removing food insecurity alone accounts for 28% of the 17-versus-14 gap pre-pandemic and 50% post-pandemic.

### Results detail relocated from the manuscript (the third recalibration step)

Explanatory prose condensed out of the Results is preserved here in full. No new result is introduced.

subsections.heading: ### Principal Findings
subsections.replacement:
A depression-screening ML model developed in Korea met its internal target (AUROC 0.836) and retained clinically useful discrimination near 0.77 on genuinely external US data and across the COVID-19 shift, with calibration recoverable by lightweight recalibration. Further modeling did not raise external discrimination.

External discrimination was 0.765 (95% CI 0.724-0.804) before the pandemic and 0.771 (0.739-0.801) after it; the difference is +0.006 (95% CI -0.045 to +0.056; bootstrap P=.86), an interval computed after the fact, and the two cycles are not distinguishable at this sample size. Calibration behaved as transportability theory predicts: the slope fell to 0.65 and 0.68 and calibration-in-the-large rose to +0.51 and +1.13, ie, systematic under-prediction of absolute risk in a higher-prevalence population. Intercept-plus-slope updating restored both without re-estimating any predictor effect, to slope 1.00 (0.95-1.00) and 1.00 (0.97-1.00), with the update refitted inside every replicate so that its own uncertainty is carried. A six-item form selected entirely inside the development data lost only 0.015 internally and 0.018 and 0.012 externally; whether triage delivered this way improves depression outcomes was not evaluated here [40]. With the threshold fixed once in the development data at 85% sensitivity and applied unchanged, external sensitivity was 0.810 and 0.791, the number needed to screen 6.8 and 4.7, and decision-curve net benefit exceeded both screen-all and screen-none defaults in every dataset.

subsections.heading: ### Comparison With Prior Work
subsections.replacement: Prior ML depression models built on Korean national surveys report strong internal performance but no external validation. Using KNHANES 2014-2018 restricted to non-smokers at risk of secondhand smoke exposure (n=11,463), Kim et al [6] classified PHQ-9 ≥10 with internal AUROC up to 0.90; using the 2023 KCHS restricted to culturally diverse families (n=2,568), Kim et al [5] predicted the continuous PHQ-9 score with a test R² of 33%. Two deliberate design choices plausibly account for the lower internal discrimination (0.836): outcome-proximal predictors such as perceived stress and single-item depressed-mood questions were excluded, and the predictor set was restricted to variables transportable to a second country; no ablation was run to attribute the difference quantitatively. The wider field supplies the same contrast: a systematic review of electronic-health-record depression models found discrimination clustered near 0.80, almost always internal [7], and among hundreds of prediction models published during the pandemic almost none were validated outside the development source [8]. An internal 0.836 is therefore unremarkable against that literature; an externally validated 0.77 in a second country has few published counterparts. That the same predictors carry more signal within Korea (0.836 internally, 0.81-0.82 at matched sample size) than in the US (near 0.77) instantiates the dataset-shift problem described for deployed clinical artificial intelligence [11,41].

subsections.heading: ### Plausible Mechanisms for the External Ceiling
subsections.replacement:
Several lines of evidence converge on concept shift as the leading explanation for the plateau near 0.77. Modeling effort is ruled out first: across 2,199 catalogued runs spanning feature engineering, hyperparameter search, ensembling, domain adaptation and deep tabular learners, no configuration selected on development-internal criteria exceeded that level, and apparent gains from externally tuned variants did not survive leakage control [42]. Estimation error is ruled out next: matching sample size did not close the gap, and increasing the training set from 0.5 to 2 million records slightly lowered external discrimination.

The most direct test was an in-domain oracle, a diagnostic upper bound rather than a candidate model. Fitting NHANES on its own labels under cluster-separated cross-validation reached just 0.764-0.776, whereas the same predictors reached 0.81-0.82 in equally sized Korean samples. The transported model sits inside the oracle's confidence interval, and therefore already performs at the level of the best model fitted on those predictors inside the external population, among the learners evaluated.

Two specification analyses locate the shortfall: at a PHQ-9 ≥5 threshold the Korea-US gap narrows from about 0.07 to about 0.02 (0.761 internally against 0.735 and 0.740 externally), and restricting training and evaluation to adults aged ≥30 years narrows it from 0.071 and 0.066 to 0.058 and 0.051; both patterns are suggestive rather than confirmatory. Predictor-importance rank order was almost unchanged between surveys (Spearman ρ=0.97 pre-pandemic and 0.99 post-pandemic). Near-identical ordering alongside external discrimination about 0.07 lower is more consistent with predictors that are the right ones but weaker externally than with a model attending to the wrong ones [43]. Measurement differences and complete-case selection cannot be separated from concept shift with these data.

subsections.heading: ### Clinical and Policy Implications
subsections.replacement:
The intended use is triage, not diagnosis; a positive score prompts confirmatory assessment rather than an action in itself. At the single development-fixed operating point, positive predictive value was 0.147 pre-pandemic and 0.214 post-pandemic, ie, 6.8 and 4.7 respondents screened per case identified, and 47% and 45% of the population were flagged for confirmatory assessment. The flag rate, not the positive predictive value, sizes the confirmatory capacity a screening program needs.

All six items of the deployment form are answerable on a single screen and need no examination, no laboratory value and no clinician; none is a symptom item, keeping the triage step distinct from the full PHQ-9. The 17-predictor version additionally needs body mass index and two physician-diagnosed conditions, which a self-completed form can only take on trust.

Any implementation outside the development population must apply local recalibration, since discrimination transported but absolute risk did not; published minimum-sample-size derivations for external validation are driven by the calibration slope rather than the AUROC [44], a constraint that binds first at a small deployment site.

Subgroup discrimination was lowest in Mexican American respondents in both NHANES cycles and, within the development population, in the highest income quintile, the one development subgroup that trips the analysis plan's 0.05 flag; the NHANES race and ethnicity intervals are wide and overlapping, leaving those differences unestablished. A deployed screener should report subgroup performance continuously [45]: the subgroup AUROC, the subgroup calibration slope, and the false-negative rate at the operating threshold, which spans 0.03 to 0.31 here (Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S7).

subsections.heading: ### Strengths and Limitations
subsections.replacement:
The principal strength is that the outcome is identical in both surveys: a nine-item PHQ-9 sum of at least 10 in KCHS and in NHANES alike, which removes the outcome-harmonization error that usually confounds cross-national validation and leaves country, health system, population composition and survey mode as the differences under test. Evaluation was complex-survey weighted throughout; a data-integrity audit and peer review corrected seven data-processing and harmonization defects before the primary analysis. No NHANES data were used in fitting, tuning or selecting the primary model, and the optimization search was leakage-controlled, which removes external-label selection as a source of optimism in the ceiling claim.

Depression-module non-response is substantial and differential, costing 7.7% of the pre-pandemic and 14.1% of the post-pandemic sample on the mobile examination center frame, counting any unanswered item (14.6% and 33.3% on the wider interview frame; Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S8), and varying by education and by race and ethnicity; the external cohorts are therefore complete-case results, and the external estimates, particularly post-pandemic subgroup results, may be biased in an unknown direction. Alcohol, physical activity, income, body mass index and food insecurity are measured differently in the two surveys and were harmonized conservatively. Every predictor value was collected by interviewer administration or in an examination center; a web or mobile form changes the mode of administration for all 17 items, an untested change. The design is cross-sectional; the model screens current symptoms rather than predicting onset. Living alone is absent from the pre-pandemic NHANES file, hence that cohort is scored as if no respondent lived alone; food insecurity is a single item in KCHS, unmeasured there in 2020 and 2021; and prior depression diagnosis is unrecorded in KCHS, precluding a diagnosis-exclusion sensitivity analysis.

Internal estimates are hold-out rather than fully cross-validated (Multimedia Appendix 1, Part B). The external cohorts carry 728 and 661 events, modest for a validation study and most limiting for calibration [44]; conditioning on a single fitted update rather than refitting it gives visibly wider slope intervals (0.82-1.19 pre and 0.88-1.13 post, Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S16). The predictor-set amendment, dated and locked before any model using the amended set was fitted, contributes a robustness analysis rather than a primary result (Multimedia Appendix 1, Part A). Two of the four hypotheses, H2 and H3, were stated qualitatively, without numeric decision margins; judging those two "supported" therefore involves interpretation.

A competing contributor is partly quantified, and it is not concept shift: the transportable predictor set is bounded by the development survey's content. Adding multimorbidity and healthcare utilization domains available in NHANES but not harmonizable to KCHS raised the in-domain oracle from 0.765 to 0.778, a 0.013 gain that is not itself evidence of signal transportable from Korea (Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S14 and Part C).

subsections.heading: ### Conclusions
subsections.replacement: A survey-derived depression screener transports across country and pandemic period with clinically useful discrimination and recoverable calibration. The cross-national ceiling near 0.77 held against every leakage-controlled attempt to exceed it and against an in-domain oracle fitted on the external labels. It is therefore best read as a property of the transportable predictor set rather than as a proven maximum, most consistent with shift in the predictor-outcome relationship and with residual contributions from differing measurement, development-survey coverage and complete-case selection. Remaining gains are more likely to come from predictor domains a development survey does not yet collect than from further algorithm search. A low-burden six-item version, paired with local recalibration and continuing subgroup monitoring, is a plausible scalable digital triage aid.

appendix_additions.markdown:
### Discussion detail relocated in revision (utility, deployment, and internal split)

Explanatory prose condensed out of the Discussion during revision is preserved here. No new result is introduced.

The parsimonious form places a low-burden self-report instrument within reach for digital triage. Whether triage delivered this way improves depression outcomes was not evaluated here; the mobile-delivery evidence base cited in Principal Findings [40] concerns intervention delivery to defined patient groups rather than the delivery of screening, and no equivalent trial evidence exists for a transported screening algorithm.

At the development-fixed operating point, weighted net benefit exceeded both the screen-all and the screen-none default strategy across the clinically relevant threshold range in every cohort (Table S3).

Development used a 500,000-record training set and a 100,001-record hold-out drawn from the 2,048,510 pooled records rather than the full pooled sample; a training-set size experiment showed this did not cost external discrimination, and internal estimates are therefore hold-out rather than fully cross-validated.

Equity requires explicit and continuing monitoring rather than an assumption that the development-time estimate holds, as recommended for machine learning intended to advance rather than erode health equity [45]. Three quantities warrant tracking: the subgroup AUROC, the subgroup calibration slope, and the false-negative rate at the operating threshold (Table S7).

### Discussion detail relocated in revision (optimization search and predictor coverage)

Explanatory prose condensed out of the Discussion during revision is preserved here. No new result is introduced.

The catalogued search also covered alternative loss functions. Leakage is the failure mode that has driven reproducibility problems across machine-learning-based science; runs screened on external labels are identified as such in Table S11. That increasing the training set from 0.5 to 2 million records slightly lowered external discrimination is a pattern consistent with source-specific overfitting rather than with an estimation-limited ceiling.

The interpretability comparison is at least consistent with the shift-stability framing of deployment failure in health artificial intelligence.

The coverage analysis extracted candidate domains available in NHANES but not harmonizable to KCHS: physician-diagnosed multimorbidity (asthma, arthritis, thyroid, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, liver disease, and cancer, excluding circulatory conditions) and healthcare utilization. KCHS records only hypertension and diabetes among physician-diagnosed conditions across more than one survey year, both already included; dyslipidemia, osteoporosis, cataract and arthritis are fielded in a single year and therefore cannot enter a model pooled over 2017-2025. KCHS collects no broader chronic-disease inventory, no hospitalization record and no visit counts, and these domains therefore cannot enter a KCHS-developed transportable model. Part of the residual external gap is thus attributable to development-survey coverage rather than to concept shift alone, and a development survey that captured multimorbidity and utilization might raise the attainable ceiling.

problems.heading: Principal Findings
problems.detail: The current text reads "decision-curve net benefit exceeded both screen-all and screen-none defaults in every dataset, with the external cohorts taken after local recalibration." The replacement drops the trailing qualifier, and the appendix3 addition repeats the claim unqualified ("weighted net benefit exceeded both the screen-all and the screen-none default strategy across the clinically relevant threshold range in every cohort (Table S3)"). A qualified statement therefore becomes unqualified in both places: as written, the reader takes the external net-benefit superiority to hold for the model as transported, when Table S3 and the Results state that the external values use intercept/slope-recalibrated probabilities.
problems.fix: With the threshold fixed once in the development data at 85% sensitivity and applied unchanged, external sensitivity was 0.810 and 0.791, the number needed to screen 6.8 and 4.7, and decision-curve net benefit exceeded both screen-all and screen-none defaults in every dataset, with the external cohorts taken after local recalibration.

problems.heading: Strengths and Limitations
problems.detail: The current limitation states the amendment "was written while the study was under way, after an earlier external result was known but before any model using the amended set was fitted." The replacement keeps only the exculpating half ("dated and locked before any model using the amended set was fitted"). The fact that the amendment was written after an earlier external result was known is the substance of the limitation; it survives only in Part A ("after the 14-predictor model had been developed and transferred") and no longer appears in the limitations at all, which softens the limitation to a statement of good practice.
problems.fix: The predictor-set amendment was written while the study was under way, after an earlier external result was known but before any model using the amended set was fitted, and contributes a robustness analysis rather than a primary result (Multimedia Appendix 1, Part A).

problems.heading: Principal Findings
problems.detail: Reference [40] is Sun et al, a randomized trial of a mobile health intervention in thyroid cancer patients. In the current text it is attached to the statement that the mobile-delivery evidence base concerns intervention delivery to defined patient groups. The replacement attaches it to "whether triage delivered this way improves depression outcomes was not evaluated here [40]," so the citation now appears to support a statement about what this study did not do. The appendix3 addition compounds this by referring back to "the mobile-delivery evidence base cited in Principal Findings [40]" when Principal Findings no longer mentions that evidence base.
problems.fix: A six-item form selected entirely inside the development data lost only 0.015 internally and 0.018 and 0.012 externally; whether triage delivered this way improves depression outcomes was not evaluated here, the available mobile-delivery trial evidence concerning intervention delivery to defined patient groups [40] rather than the delivery of screening.

problems.heading: Plausible Mechanisms for the External Ceiling
problems.detail: Reference [43] is Subbaswamy and Saria on dataset shift and shift-stable models. In the current text it supports the framing sentence ("a pattern that is at least consistent with the shift-stability framing of deployment failure in health artificial intelligence [43]"). The replacement moves [43] onto the empirical inference that the predictors are the right ones but weaker externally, a claim the reference does not support, while the appendix4 addition restates the shift-stability framing with no citation at all.
problems.fix: Near-identical ordering alongside external discrimination about 0.07 lower is more consistent with predictors that are the right ones but weaker externally than with a model attending to the wrong ones, a pattern at least consistent with the shift-stability framing of deployment failure in health artificial intelligence [43].

problems.heading: Plausible Mechanisms for the External Ceiling
problems.detail: The current text says the two specification analyses "place the shortfall at the moderate-or-worse end of the symptom distribution and among the youngest adults." The replacement opens with "Two specification analyses locate the shortfall:" and then never states where the shortfall is located; the localization appears in neither appendix addition (the existing appendix4 block likewise says only "locate where the shortfall sits"). The sentence asserts a localization whose content has been deleted.
problems.fix: Two specification analyses locate the shortfall at the moderate-or-worse end of the symptom distribution and among the youngest adults: at a PHQ-9 ≥5 threshold the Korea-US gap narrows from about 0.07 to about 0.02 (0.761 internally against 0.735 and 0.740 externally), and restricting training and evaluation to adults aged ≥30 years narrows it from 0.071 and 0.066 to 0.058 and 0.051; both patterns are suggestive rather than confirmatory.

problems.heading: Strengths and Limitations
problems.detail: The current text ends the calibration-precision limitation with "a deployment that fits its update once on a modest local sample is in that wider regime." The replacement reports the wider conditional intervals but drops the clause that says which deployments they apply to, and neither appendix addition carries it (the existing appendix3 block covers only that the local sample size for a stable update was not examined). The limitation loses its scope: the nested-versus-conditional distinction is left as a technical aside rather than a statement about real deployments.
problems.fix: The external cohorts carry 728 and 661 events, modest for a validation study and most limiting for calibration [44]; conditioning on a single fitted update rather than refitting it gives visibly wider slope intervals (0.82-1.19 pre and 0.88-1.13 post, Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S16), and a deployment that fits its update once on a modest local sample is in that wider regime.

problems.heading: Comparison With Prior Work
problems.detail: The current caveat is "no ablation was run to attribute the difference quantitatively across studies that differ in population and outcome scale." The replacement keeps "no ablation was run to attribute the difference quantitatively" but drops the clause identifying why the comparison is not like-for-like. Since the two cited studies used restricted populations and, in one case, a continuous outcome, removing that clause widens the comparison into an apples-to-apples contrast that the data do not support.
problems.fix: Two deliberate design choices plausibly account for the lower internal discrimination (0.836): outcome-proximal predictors such as perceived stress and single-item depressed-mood questions were excluded, and the predictor set was restricted to variables transportable to a second country; no ablation was run to attribute the difference quantitatively across studies that differ in population and outcome scale.

sections.verdict: Revise before splicing. The cut is sound in structure - the relocations to Part B and Part C are accurate, the cited tables (S3, S7, S11, S14, S16) hold the content attributed to them, and the DO NOT LOSE items that fall in the Discussion (living alone absent pre-pandemic, no NHANES data in fitting/tuning/selection, oracle as diagnostic upper bound with the transported model inside its interval, substantial and differential depression-module non-response with complete-case external cohorts, H2/H3 qualitative-verdict caveat) all survive. Seven problems need correcting: two qualifications that became unqualified claims (external net benefit taken after recalibration; the not-like-for-like caveat on the prior-work comparison), one limitation materially softened (the amendment timing relative to a known earlier external result), two citations moved onto claims the sources do not support ([40], [43]), and two deleted contents whose introducing sentences still promise them (where the shortfall is located; which deployments sit in the wider calibration-slope regime).
